## Can vessel networks help personalize treatment?

::: {.motivation-grid}
::: {.story-card}
<div class="card-kicker">THE TREATMENT</div>
<p>Neoadjuvant therapy is given before surgery to shrink the tumor.</p>
:::

::: {.story-card .feature-card}
<div class="card-kicker">THE OUTCOME</div>
<p>About 1 in 3 exams came from patients who achieved a **pathologic complete response** (pCR): no invasive cancer remained in the breast or nearby lymph nodes at surgery. Achieving pCR is associated with better long-term outcomes.</p>
:::

::: {.story-card}
<div class="card-kicker">THE QUESTION</div>
<p>A **graph neural network**, or **GNN**, learns from both measurements at vessel locations and the connections between them. Can a GNN use connections within breast vessel networks to improve treatment-response prediction?</p>
:::
:::

Earlier prediction could guide less intensive therapy for patients likely to achieve pCR and alternative therapy for those unlikely to do so.

::: {.notes}
Neoadjuvant therapy is a treatment given before surgery, typically chemotherapy.
At surgery, if no invasive cancer remains in the breast or the surrounding lymph
nodes, this is called pCR. pCR is associated with improved outcomes. We ask
whether modeling the vascular network as a graph improves pCR prediction over
the same measurements without those connections. Earlier
prediction could guide less intensive therapy for patients likely to achieve pCR
and alternative therapy for those unlikely to do so.
:::

## Tumors build a messier blood supply

::: {.image-row}
![](figures/vessels_normal.png){.nostretch height="300px" fig-align="center"}

![](figures/vessels_tumor.png){.nostretch height="300px" fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.result-grid}
::: {.result-card}
<strong>Normal vessels: organized, efficient.</strong>

Blood flows through a predictable, well-structured network.
:::

::: {.result-card .caution}
<strong>Tumor vessels: dense, tortuous, leaky.</strong>

Tumors stimulate abnormal vessel growth as they grow. Structure may reflect tumor biology and treatment sensitivity.
:::
:::

Because tumor vessels differ in both structure and blood flow, those patterns may help predict treatment response.

::: {.image-credit}
Vessel diagrams from *Nature Medicine*, Jain RK, "Molecular regulation of vessel maturation", 2003;9(6):685&ndash;693,^15^ copyright (2003).
:::

::: {.notes}
Why might vessels carry predictive signal? Well, healthy blood vessels are
organized, and blood flows through them efficiently. Meanwhile tumors stimulate
new growth, which is often dense, tortuous, and leaky. To see any of this on MRI
we inject a metal-based dye called contrast into the blood, which is what makes
the vessels light up. That structure, and the way contrast flows through it, may
reflect tumor biology and sensitivity to treatment — which is why we expect it
to help predict pCR.
:::

## Ultrafast MRI captures images every few seconds as contrast enters tissue

![](figures/movie_curves.svg){.nostretch width="80%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.aside-note .centered}
Curves are from different patients and are shown only to compare temporal sampling.
:::

::: {.three-facts}
<div><strong>179</strong><span>pCR-labeled exams, 141 patients</span></div>
<div><strong>1,226</strong><span>pCR-unlabeled exams, pretraining only</span></div>
<div><strong>13–24</strong><span>frames per ultrafast movie</span></div>
:::

::: {.notes}
Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, or DCE-MRI, repeatedly images the breast before
and after that contrast injection. As contrast reaches vessels and tissue, their
MRI signal changes over time.

Conventional DCE-MRI samples this enhancement relatively slowly: roughly every
two minutes in the protocol shown here. Ultrafast DCE-MRI acquires a 3D volume
every few seconds, allowing us to observe the early wash-in of contrast.

The dots show when each protocol measures enhancement at a vessel location.
Conventional DCE-MRI captures only a few measurements, while ultrafast DCE-MRI
samples every few seconds and resolves early wash-in.

Our data contains 179 exams from 141 patients, and another 1,226 exams without
treatment-response labels.

The acquisition protocols aren't uniform: exams contain 13 to 24 frames, and
their cadence and duration also vary. I'll return to why that matters.
:::

## The GNN first predicts later MRI frames, then predicts treatment response

![](figures/arch5.svg){.nostretch width="100%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
So, walking briefly through the pipeline: The inputs are ultrafast images, frame
timings, and one-voxel-wide vessel centerlines. I convert the centerlines into
graphs: vessel locations become nodes, and connected locations share an edge. The
green box is the heart of the GNN: a graph convolution, intended to capture
spatial information, and a recurrent unit, intended to capture temporal
structure.

In pretraining, the model learns to predict future enhancement at connected
vessel nodes. The target comes from the scan itself, so it needs no human labels
— that is what lets us use all 1,226 unlabeled exams. Those weights then
initialize the encoder for a pCR prediction head, and fine tuning uses the
expensive labeled data.

Crucially, we run the same recipe on a matched model with the vessel connections
removed — from scratch and pretrained — and evaluate everything with whole
patients held out. So: does the graph help? Does pretraining?
:::

## Learning to predict later MRI frames improved the GNN

![](figures/results_auc.svg){.nostretch width="54%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.result-grid}
::: {.result-card}
<strong>Pretraining helped.</strong>

Learning to predict later MRI frames improved the GNN by **0.149 AUC** (95% CI, 0.046&ndash;0.255). After pretraining, the GNN also outperformed the matched graph-free model by **0.079** (95% CI, 0.010&ndash;0.155).
:::

::: {.result-card .caution}
<strong>But scan timing was associated with pCR too.</strong>

A model using only scan-timing information, no imaging, reached **AUC 0.587** (95% CI, 0.483&ndash;0.686), and its predictions correlated with the GNN's at **r = 0.50**. We don't yet know why; next we need to determine what drives that association and whether it influences the GNN's predictions.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The answer is that pretraining helped. For the GNN it was worth 0.149 AUC, with a
confidence interval from about 0.05 to 0.26. The effect was smaller for the
graph-free model, at 0.03, and there the interval included zero — so we cannot
distinguish it from no effect.

After pretraining, the GNN did beat the graph-free model, by 0.08 AUC. But all
four models' absolute AUCs had confidence intervals straddling 0.5, which is
chance: the improvements are measurable, but no model is clearly better than
guessing.

And remember how the number of frames was heterogeneous across exams? I tested
that directly. A model given only scan timing — frame count, duration, cadence,
no imaging at all — reached 0.587, essentially the pretrained GNN's 0.583, and
the two models' predictions correlate at r = 0.5. Scan timing is associated with
outcome in this cohort; we cannot yet tell whether that reflects the scans or the
patients.
:::

## Summary

::: {.remember-grid}
::: {.remember-card}
<span>1</span>
<p>Learning to predict later MRI frames <strong>improved the GNN.</strong></p>
:::

::: {.remember-card}
<span>2</span>
<p>With pretraining, the GNN outperformed the model that <strong>ignored vessel connections.</strong></p>
:::

::: {.remember-card}
<span>3</span>
<p>How the scans were timed also predicted pCR, so we need to learn whether the model is detecting <strong>tumor biology or scan differences.</strong></p>
:::
:::

<div class="closing-line">Learning to predict contrast changes improved the GNN, but some of its signal may come from how the scans were collected.</div>

::: {.notes}
So in conclusion, I built a graph neural network to predict treatment response,
and pretraining it to forecast contrast in future frames improved it over random
initialization. In this analysis, the pretrained GNN outperformed the matched
model that ignored vessel connections, suggesting that vascular connectivity may
add information beyond each vessel location's enhancement curve alone. However,
because scan timing also predicted outcome, we can't yet attribute that signal
specifically to vascular biology — and separating the two is the next step.
:::
